Short description: Ballast replacement and fluorescent repair, with a straight comparison of repair versus LED conversion on real numbers.
Post body:
Ballast Replacement and Fluorescent Lighting Repair in the Phoenix Valley

Flickering tubes, a persistent hum, or a fixture that takes three tries to come on are all the same conversation: the ballast is going. At The Wire Guy Electric, we repair and replace fluorescent lighting for commercial spaces across the Valley, and we will tell you honestly when repair is the wrong call.

Signs the Ballast Is Failing

  • Tubes that flicker or strobe, especially when first switched on
  • An audible hum or buzz from the fixture
  • Slow starting, or tubes that need a moment before they light
  • Dim or inconsistent output across a fixture
  • Discoloration at the tube ends
  • New tubes that fail quickly, which usually means the ballast, not the tubes
  • Any oily residue or burnt smell from the housing

Repair or Convert to LED?

This is the real decision, and it is worth thinking about rather than defaulting.

Replacing a ballast makes sense when you have a small number of failures in a fixture set that is otherwise in good shape, or when budget timing means a full conversion has to wait.

Converting to LED usually makes more sense when you are replacing ballasts repeatedly across a space, when the fixtures are old enough that more failures are certain, or when the space has high ceilings where every service call means a lift. In that last case the labor of ongoing maintenance frequently outweighs the cost of converting.

There is also a hard reality worth planning around: fluorescent lamp and ballast availability has been shrinking, and specific tube types get harder to source over time. If your building depends on a type that is being phased down, converting on your schedule beats converting in an emergency. More on our commercial LED lighting page.

How We Work in Occupied Spaces

Lighting work is disruptive by nature since the lights go out to do it. We schedule around business hours, work area by area, and keep the space usable throughout. For a full-building sweep, doing it in one coordinated visit is cheaper and less disruptive than handling failures one at a time as they happen.

Short description: Dead circuits, repeat trips, voltage problems, overheating terminations, and the intermittent faults nobody else can pin down.
Post body:
Commercial Electrical Troubleshooting in the Phoenix Valley

When a circuit goes down in a business, the clock starts immediately. Product is warming, the line is stopped, the register is dead, or a suite full of people has nothing to do. At The Wire Guy Electric, we diagnose commercial electrical faults across the Valley and fix the cause rather than the symptom.

What We Diagnose

  • Dead circuits and partial outages where the breaker never tripped
  • Breakers that trip repeatedly, especially under load or at the same time each day
  • Equipment that keeps failing, which is often a supply problem rather than an equipment problem
  • Voltage problems, including drops under load and imbalance across phases
  • Overheating at panels, disconnects, and terminations
  • Lighting that flickers or drops out in sections
  • Nuisance GFCI tripping
  • Intermittent faults, the ones that never happen while anybody is looking

How We Approach It

Commercial systems are harder to trace than residential ones because there is more of everything: more distribution, more panels, more circuits that were added over the years by people who did not label anything.

So the first job is usually understanding what is actually there. We map the distribution, identify what is on the affected circuit, and test methodically from the load back toward the source. Thermal inspection is useful here, because heat shows up at a failing connection well before it fails outright.

The common causes are consistent: loose or corroded terminations, a failing breaker, an undersized circuit that has quietly been overloaded since somebody added equipment, a damaged conductor, or a neutral problem on a shared circuit.

Intermittent Problems

These are the frustrating ones, and they are also the ones most worth solving properly. A fault that appears only under load, or only in the afternoon heat, is telling you something specific: something is marginal and temperature or current is pushing it over the line.

Those almost always get worse. Finding them while they are intermittent is considerably cheaper than finding them after they take equipment or a full circuit down.

What Should Not Wait

  • Any burning smell near a panel, disconnect, or piece of equipment
  • A panel or disconnect that is warm, buzzing, or discolored
  • Scorch marks at any termination
  • Repeated breaker trips on a circuit serving critical equipment
  • Any shock reported by staff

Name: Dedicated Circuits
Short description: Dedicated circuits for commercial equipment. Kitchen, refrigeration, medical, salon, and server loads sized off the nameplate.
Post body:
Dedicated Circuits for Commercial Equipment in the Phoenix Valley

A dedicated circuit serves one piece of equipment and nothing else. It sounds like a small distinction. In practice it is the difference between equipment that runs reliably for years and equipment that keeps tripping, keeps failing, and keeps costing you service calls. At The Wire Guy Electric, we design and install dedicated circuits for commercial equipment across the Valley.

When Equipment Needs Its Own Circuit

  • Anything with a compressor or a motor. Refrigeration, walk-ins, air compressors, and HVAC draw a large surge at startup that drags voltage down for everything sharing the circuit.
  • Commercial kitchen equipment. Ovens, fryers, warmers, dishwashers, and ice machines.
  • Medical and dental equipment, including autoclaves and imaging.
  • Salon equipment, dryers and processors that pull hard and continuously.
  • Server racks, network gear, and point of sale. These are sensitive to what everything else on the circuit is doing.
  • Shop machinery and anything with a duty cycle.

What Sharing Actually Costs You

Two things go wrong when equipment shares a circuit it should not.

The first is nuisance tripping. Total draw exceeds the breaker when two things happen to run at once, usually at the worst possible time, and staff learn to reset the breaker as a routine rather than report it.

The second is quieter and more expensive. Motor startups cause voltage dips, and sensitive electronics on the same circuit see those dips. That shows up as equipment that reboots, corrupts data, or simply fails early for no visible reason. Nobody connects it back to the compressor cycling in the back room, but that is often exactly what is happening.

How We Size It

Off the equipment nameplate, every time. The nameplate gives the minimum circuit ampacity and the maximum overcurrent protection, and that is what the conductor and breaker get sized to, not a rule of thumb.

Continuous loads need additional headroom. Long runs need conductor sizing that accounts for voltage drop, which matters more than people expect in a warehouse. And in Arizona, ambient temperature derating is real: a conductor run through an uninsulated roof space is not operating at the temperature the base table assumes.

  • Load calculation on your existing panel before we promise a number. An 80-amp charger on an already-loaded 200-amp panel is a problem waiting to happen.
  • Correct wire gauge. Undersized wire is a fire hazard, especially in Phoenix heat. We size per NEC 2023 tables with AZ ambient derating.
  • Dedicated circuit and properly sized breaker. No piggy-backing on existing circuits.
  • GFCI protection where required by code.
  • Clean conduit routing. Interior conduit hidden where possible, UV-rated exterior conduit where exposed to sun.
  • A charger that hits its rated speed. An undersized circuit means a charger that quietly throttles. We size for the charge rate you paid for.

Short description: Inspections for home buyers, sellers, and older homes. Panel, wiring, GFCI, and grounding assessed with real pricing on every finding.
Post body:
Electrical Safety Inspections in the Phoenix Valley

Most people call us for an inspection at one of three moments: they are buying a house, they are selling one and an inspector flagged something, or something in their current home has started behaving badly enough to worry them. At The Wire Guy Electric, an inspection is a real assessment of what is actually in your walls and panel, not a sales walkthrough.

When an Inspection Is Worth It

  • Buying a home. A general home inspector flags obvious problems. An electrician tells you what the panel, the service, and the wiring actually are, and what they will cost you.
  • You have an inspection report already. Bring it to us. We will price out the electrical items on it and tell you honestly which ones matter and which are boilerplate.
  • The house is more than 30 years old and nobody has looked at the electrical since.
  • Before a large addition, like a pool, casita, EV charger, or second AC system.
  • Something is off. Flickering, warm outlets, repeat trips, or a panel you have never liked the look of.

What We Look At

The panel and service. Brand and age, condition of the bus and lugs, breaker sizing against the conductors they protect, grounding and bonding, available capacity, and whether the panel is on the recall list. Federal Pacific, Zinsco, Challenger, and Pushmatic all get flagged, and we explain why in our post on Federal Pacific and Zinsco panels in Arizona.

The wiring. What type it is and what condition it is in where we can see it. In homes from the 1960s and 1970s that includes checking for single strand aluminum branch wiring, which is a genuine fire risk at connections and needs proper treatment.

Devices and protection. GFCI protection where it is required, especially kitchens, baths, garages, and exteriors. Arc-fault protection. Grounded versus ungrounded receptacles, and three-prong outlets that were installed on two-wire circuits with no ground behind them.

The parts nobody looks at. Attic junctions, exterior disconnects, the meter base, and outdoor equipment that has been baking in the sun since the house was built.

What You Get

A clear list of what we found, sorted by what actually matters. Safety items that should be handled now, items worth planning for, and items that are simply worth knowing about. Plus real numbers for the work, so you can make decisions instead of guessing.

We are not going to hand you a list of everything technically imperfect in a forty-year-old house and call it urgent. Most older Valley homes have a handful of things worth fixing and a lot of things that are simply old. Knowing which is which is the point of hiring us.

  • Local context. We know what the housing stock in Mesa, Tempe, and Scottsdale actually has in it by era.

Commercial Electrical Upgrades in the Phoenix Valley

Most commercial buildings in the Valley were wired for the business that was in them thirty years ago. Then the use changed, the equipment changed, and the electrical stayed exactly the same. At The Wire Guy Electric, we handle the upgrades that bring a building's electrical up to what the business actually needs now.

What We Upgrade

  • Feeders. Undersized feeders to a suite or a piece of equipment are a common finding and a real constraint.
  • Equipment circuits for new machinery, kitchen equipment, compressors, and server rooms.
  • Lighting and controls, usually alongside an LED conversion.

Start With the Load Calculation

Every one of these projects should begin with real math rather than an assumption. A load calculation tells you what the service can carry, what is actually connected, and how much headroom is left.

That matters because the answer is frequently better than expected. Plenty of buildings have adequate service and a distribution problem, which is a much smaller project than a service upgrade. Finding that out first saves real money.

When the service genuinely is the constraint, knowing early lets you plan the utility coordination and the downtime instead of discovering it the week new equipment arrives.

Post body:
Emergency and Exit Lighting in the Phoenix Valley

Exit and emergency lighting is the system nobody thinks about until an inspection or an actual emergency, and it is also the system most likely to be quietly non-functional. The fixture on the wall looks fine. The battery inside it died two years ago. At The Wire Guy Electric, we install, test, and repair egress lighting for commercial properties across the Valley.

What We Handle

  • Exit sign installation and placement along egress paths
  • Emergency lighting, both the classic twin-head units and integrated fixtures with battery backup
  • Battery replacement, which is the single most common repair on these systems
  • Testing and correcting whatever fails it
  • Replacing dead or damaged units
  • Retrofits of old incandescent exit signs to LED, which cut standby draw substantially across a building with many signs
  • Adding coverage where a layout change left a path unlit

Why These Fail Quietly

The fixture is powered and the indicator light is on, so everything appears fine. But the indicator only tells you the unit is receiving power. It does not tell you the battery still holds a charge, which is the only thing that matters when the power goes out.

Batteries have a finite service life, and Arizona heat shortens it. A unit mounted in a warehouse, a stairwell, or anywhere near a roof deck sees ambient temperatures that age a battery considerably faster than the spec sheet assumes.

This is why the only real test is the actual test: kill power to the unit and confirm it illuminates for the required duration. That is a straightforward thing to do on a schedule and the single best way to avoid finding out during an inspection.

Layout Changes Create Gaps

Something we find often: a building's egress lighting was correct when it was installed, then a tenant improvement moved walls, added a corridor, or changed the exit path. The lighting stayed where it was.

Any time a space gets reconfigured, the egress path and its lighting should be reviewed against the new layout. If you are planning a buildout, that belongs in scope from the start. See our tenant improvement page.

Exterior Electrical in the Phoenix Valley

Outdoor electrical in Arizona is a different job than outdoor electrical anywhere else. Everything you install lives in direct sun at 115 degrees, gets sandblasted by haboob dust, then takes sideways rain for two months of monsoon. Equipment that would last twenty years in a mild climate gives up here in five. At The Wire Guy Electric, we build exterior work to survive that, not just to pass a first look.

What We Install Outside

  • Exterior outlets and GFCI receptacles in weatherproof in-use covers, which is the only kind that actually protects a cord that stays plugged in.
  • Landscape and path lighting, including transformer sizing and burial depth done properly so the run does not fail at the first splice.
  • Security and flood lighting, motion sensing, dusk-to-dawn photocells, and camera power.
  • Patio, pergola, and ramada power for fans, heaters, TVs, and misting systems.
  • Detached structures. Feeders and subpanels for garages, shops, casitas, and sheds.
  • Pool and spa equipment circuits, including bonding and disconnects.
  • Gate, well, and irrigation controller power.
  • EV charger circuits routed on exterior walls. More on our EV charger installation page.

Why Outdoor Work Fails Here

Almost every exterior repair we get called for traces back to one of four things.

UV. Standard PVC and non-rated cable go chalky and brittle in Arizona sun. We use UV-rated conduit and fittings on anything exposed, because the sun finds everything else.

Water intrusion. A cover that is weatherproof only when closed does nothing for the cord you leave plugged in year-round. In-use covers and correct fitting orientation are what keep water out of a box.

Bad splices underground. Landscape lighting is where we find the worst of it: wire nuts buried in dirt, no direct-burial connectors, no protection at all. Those work for one season.

Undersized runs. Long runs to a back-yard structure lose voltage. Lights dim, motors run hot, equipment wears out early. That is a wire-sizing decision, made once, at install.

Landscape Lighting Worth Paying For

Good landscape lighting is a design job as much as an electrical one: light the trees and the architecture, hide the fixtures, and avoid the runway-of-path-lights look. We plan the layout with you, size the transformer with headroom for expansion, and use direct-burial rated connections throughout. Cost detail is in our landscape lighting cost guide.

Light Fixture Replacement in the Phoenix Valley

Swapping a light fixture looks like a fifteen-minute job until you get the old one down and find out what is behind it. At The Wire Guy Electric, fixture replacement is one of our most common calls, and a good share of them turn into a conversation about the box, the wiring, or the switch rather than the fixture itself.

What We Replace

  • Ceiling fixtures and flush mounts throughout the house
  • Chandeliers in entries, dining rooms, and stairwells, which usually need a rated box and real bracing
  • Pendants over islands and nooks, hung level and spaced correctly
  • Vanity and bath fixtures, including wet-rated units over tubs and showers
  • Ceiling fans, which need a fan-rated box every time, not the box that was already there
  • Exterior fixtures, sconces, and flood lights
  • Old fluorescent kitchen boxes swapped for recessed cans or modern flush mounts

What We Find When the Old Fixture Comes Down

This is the part worth knowing before you buy a fixture.

The box is not rated for the weight. A heavy chandelier or a fan on a standard plastic box is a real failure risk. Fans especially, because vibration works fasteners loose over years.

The wiring is brittle. In older Valley homes, decades of heat in an attic makes conductor insulation crack right at the box, exactly where it gets flexed during a swap.

There is no ground. Older two-wire circuits are common in homes wired before grounding was standard, and it changes what can safely be installed.

The dimmer does not match the fixture. The most frequent complaint we hear after a DIY swap is buzzing or flickering LEDs. That is almost always an old dimmer designed for incandescent load trying to run an LED driver.

Bringing Your Own Fixture

Most people do, and that is fine. Two things help: have it on site before we arrive, and open the box to check the parts are all there. If you want a second opinion on whether something will look right in the space or work with your ceiling, ask before you buy. We would rather tell you up front than after it is hanging.

When a Swap Is Not the Right Answer

Sometimes the fixture is not the problem. If a room is dim because it has one central light and no other sources, a better fixture will not fix that. Recessed cans, or a layered plan with task and accent light, is the actual answer. Details on our custom lighting page and our recessed lighting page.

  • Dimmer compatibility handled. No buzz, no flicker, no guessing.

Commercial Pendant and Hanging Light Installation in the Phoenix Valley

Hanging fixtures do more visual work than any other lighting in a commercial space. What Separates a Good Install

Support that is actually rated. Commercial fixtures get heavy, and a decorative fixture over a dining area is not a place to find out the box was not rated for it. We install proper support and bracing, and in a drop ceiling that means tying into structure above rather than the grid.

Height and spacing. Too low over a bar and people hit them. Too high and the fixture stops doing its job. Spacing has to relate to the furniture below, which means it should be set after the layout is known.

Level and aligned. A run of pendants that is not level or evenly spaced is the first thing a customer notices, even if they could not tell you why the room feels off.

Dimming that works. Restaurants and hospitality spaces change atmosphere through the day. Driver and dimmer compatibility has to be checked, because mismatched components mean buzzing or flicker at low levels.

Working With Your Designer

Plenty of these projects come with a designer or architect already specifying fixtures. That works well, and the earlier we see the spec the better. The two things worth flagging before an order goes in are the weight and support requirements, and whether the fixture's driver will play nicely with the dimming system in the space. Both are cheap to solve before purchase and awkward after.

Recessed Lighting Installation in the Phoenix Valley

Recessed lighting is the single most requested upgrade we do. It takes a room lit by one dim fixture in the middle of the ceiling and makes it feel finished. Done well, you stop noticing the lights and start noticing the room. Done poorly, you get a grid of hot spots and dark corners. At The Wire Guy Electric, the difference is in the layout, and the layout is free to get right at the planning stage.

Layout Is the Whole Job

Most bad recessed installs are bad because somebody spaced the cans evenly across a ceiling without thinking about what is under them.

We plan around how the room is used. Cans pulled off the walls far enough to avoid scalloping. Spacing set by ceiling height rather than a fixed number. Light placed over the counters, the seating, and the work surfaces instead of the middle of the walkway. Wall washing where there is art or a feature wall.

In a kitchen this matters most, because standing at your own counter in your own shadow is the most common complaint we hear about a lighting job somebody else did.

Getting the Light Itself Right

  • Color temperature. 2700K reads warm and residential. 3000K is a clean neutral most people like in kitchens and baths. Above that starts feeling like an office. Consistency across a room matters more than the exact number.
  • Dimming. Worth it on almost every install. A kitchen at full output at 9 p.m. is unpleasant, and dimmers cost very little at install time.
  • Beam spread and trim. Baffle trims cut glare. Adjustable trims aim light at art or a wall.
  • IC rating. Required anywhere a can contacts insulation, which in a Valley attic is most of them.
  • Wet and damp rating for showers, soffits, and covered patios.

Retrofit into an Existing Ceiling

Two-story ceilings and vaulted or coffered ceilings take more planning, and second-floor rooms with a floor above rather than an attic are the ones worth walking before quoting.

We are careful about what we cut into. Joists, ducting, and existing runs are all up there, and finding them first is the difference between a clean install and a drywall repair.

Kitchen and Bathroom Remodel Electrical in the Phoenix Valley

Kitchens and baths are the two remodels we do most, and they are also the two where the electrical is most likely to be underestimated. Once the cabinets come off the wall and the tile comes up, what is behind them is frequently not what anybody assumed. At The Wire Guy Electric, we do remodel electrical for homeowners, designers, and general contractors across Mesa, Scottsdale, Gilbert, Chandler, Tempe, and Queen Creek.

What a Kitchen Actually Needs

A modern kitchen is one of the densest electrical spaces in a house, and older Valley kitchens were not built for it. A typical remodel involves:

  • Small appliance circuits serving the countertop receptacles, which in most older kitchens means adding circuits rather than reusing what is there
  • Dedicated circuits for the refrigerator, dishwasher, disposal, and microwave
  • A 240-volt range or cooktop circuit, sized to the appliance, plus a separate circuit if the wall oven is going somewhere else
  • GFCI protection on countertop and island receptacles, and arc-fault protection where required
  • Island and peninsula power, which has to be planned with the cabinet maker because there is often only one workable location
  • Lighting in layers: recessed for general light, pendants over the island, and under-cabinet for the counters

Under-cabinet lighting is worth doing properly rather than with a hardware store kit. We cut and solder continuous runs to fit each cabinet and hardwire them to a switch or dimmer, so there are no gaps, no visible cords, and no plug-in drivers. Details on our custom lighting page.

What a Bathroom Actually Needs

  • GFCI protection on all receptacles, which is the single most common thing missing in older Valley bathrooms
  • A dedicated circuit for the receptacles, separate from the lighting
  • Proper exhaust ventilation, correctly sized and vented outside rather than into the attic, on a timer or humidity sensor
  • Vanity lighting placed to light a face rather than the top of a head, which is a fixture-placement decision made at rough-in
  • Wet-rated fixtures in and over showers and tubs
  • Heated floor and mirror circuits, if those are in the plan, because both need to be run before tile

The Panel Question

A kitchen remodel usually adds several circuits to a house. If your panel is full, or already carrying an AC system and an EV charger, that is a conversation to have at the start of the project rather than the middle.

Sometimes the answer is a subpanel. Sometimes it is a replacement. For reference, a standard 200-amp like-for-like panel replacement in the Valley generally runs $5,200 to $6,500, and a full service replacement with a new all-in-one meter base and panel is typically $6,400 to $8,750. Not every remodel triggers one. But finding out at demo is much better than finding out the week the cabinets arrive. More on our panel replacement page.

What We Find Behind Old Walls

Open walls are the only time some of this is visible, and remodels are when we catch it:

  • Single strand aluminum branch wiring in homes wired in the 1960s and 1970s, which is a genuine fire risk at connections and should be addressed while the walls are open. We wrote about it in detail here: aluminum wiring in older Phoenix homes.
  • Ungrounded two-wire circuits feeding outlets that somebody replaced with three-prong receptacles
  • Junction boxes buried in walls with no access, which is both a code problem and a reliability problem
  • Circuits daisy-chained across rooms in ways that make no sense until you map them
  • Backstabbed devices that have been loosening for thirty years

None of this is a reason to panic. All of it is dramatically cheaper to fix while the walls are already open, which is the entire argument for handling it now.

Beyond Kitchens and Baths

We do the rest of it too: whole-house remodels, laundry rooms, garage conversions, casita and guest suite buildouts, home offices that need real circuits, and additions. The approach is the same. Electrical Troubleshooting in Mesa and the Phoenix Valley

Something is not working and nobody can tell you why. A room went dead. Half the outlets in the kitchen quit. The lights dim every time the AC starts. A breaker trips at the same time every evening and nobody can find the cause. At The Wire Guy Electric, troubleshooting is the work we are best at, because it is the work that rewards actually knowing what you are looking at.

What We Get Called For

  • Part of the house has no power and the breaker is not tripped
  • A breaker trips repeatedly, sometimes on a schedule, sometimes only in the heat
  • Outlets that quit, usually a whole run of them at once
  • Lights that flicker or dim when large appliances start
  • Burning smells, warm outlets, or a warm panel, which is the one to call about today
  • Buzzing from a switch, fixture, panel, or disconnect
  • GFCIs that will not reset
  • Shocks or tingles from an appliance or fixture

How We Actually Find It

Most electrical faults are not where the symptom is. A dead bedroom outlet is often caused by a failed connection in a completely different room, because outlets are wired in runs and the break is upstream of what you noticed.

So we map the circuit rather than guess at it. We identify what is actually on the affected circuit, test where power stops, and work back to the fault. That usually lands on one of a short list: a backstabbed device that has loosened over decades, a junction connection cooked by heat, a failing breaker, a damaged conductor, or a shared neutral doing something it should not.

The reason this matters: replacing the outlet you can see does nothing if the problem is a connection two rooms away. That fix appears to work and fails again a month later.

Why Valley Homes Fail in Specific Ways

Arizona heat is hard on connections. Attic temperatures cycle brutally every day for months, conductors expand and contract, and connections that were merely adequate at install work themselves loose. Loose connections generate heat, and heat accelerates the process. That is why so many of our summer calls are intermittent problems that get worse in the afternoon.

Dust and monsoon moisture take care of the exterior side, and homes wired in the 1960s and 1970s can carry single strand aluminum branch wiring, which needs proper treatment at every connection. We cover that in our post on aluminum wiring in older Phoenix homes.

Call Today, Not Next Week, If You Have These

  • A burning or hot-plastic smell anywhere near a panel, outlet, or fixture
  • An outlet or switch plate that is warm or discolored
  • Scorch marks around a receptacle
  • A panel that buzzes, or that is warm to the touch
  • Any shock, even a small one, from an appliance or fixture

Those are not wait-and-see items. Our post on panels that are hot to the touch explains why.

A new Valley home is not the load profile of a 1995 home. Between two AC systems, a pool, a spa, one or two EV chargers, a casita, a shop, and eventually a battery, the connected load adds up fast. A 200-amp service is the baseline we build around for most custom homes, and we run the calculation against what the house will look like in ten years rather than move-in day.

The relevant number for comparison: adding capacity later, once the drywall is up and the meter is set, means a panel or full service replacement that generally runs $5,200 to $6,500 for a standard 200-amp like-for-like, or $6,400 to $8,750 for a full service replacement with a new all-in-one meter base and panel. Doing it correctly during construction costs a fraction of that. Our panel replacement page covers what that work involves when it does have to happen after the fact.

Rough-In Is Your Last Cheap Change Order

We walk the house with the homeowner at rough-in, before insulation, and it is the most valuable hour of the project. Standing in the framed space, people see things the plan never showed them: the switch on the wrong side of the door, the outlet the future desk needs, the pendant spacing over an island that is wider than it looked on paper, the missing floor outlet in a great room with no walls near the seating.

Moving a box at that stage takes minutes. Moving it in April after the walls are painted is a drywall repair, a texture match, and a paint call.

Things We Plan For in Arizona Specifically

  • Attic heat. A Valley attic runs brutally hot for months. Conductor sizing accounts for ambient derating rather than a chart pulled from a milder climate.
  • Block and stucco. Exterior runs get planned before the block goes up, not chased into it afterward.
  • Casitas, shops, and detached garages. Feeders and subpanels sized for what actually goes in them, including a mini-split and a compressor rather than a light and a receptacle.
  • Pool and spa equipment. Bonding, disconnects, and circuits planned with the pool contractor instead of after they show up.
  • EV ready. Even for people who do not own an EV yet, a conduit and a panel space during construction costs almost nothing. See our EV charger installation page.
  • Solar and battery ready. Panel space and location planned so a future install does not require moving equipment.

Lighting Is Worth Doing Deliberately

Most new homes get a generic can layout on a grid. The houses that look genuinely finished got a lighting plan: layered ambient, task, and accent, dimmers where they matter, and cabinet and cove lighting built in rather than added later. That is work we specialize in, and rough-in is the only time it is easy. Details on our custom lighting page.

Why Builders and Homeowners Choose Us

  • We bid from plans and hold the number.
  • We hit rough-in dates. Framing, insulation, and drywall are all stacked behind us and we know it.
  • Clean work that inspects well. Straight runs, proper support, correct torque, labeled panel.
  • We talk to homeowners like adults. If a request is a bad idea, you hear why, along with a better option.
  • Licensed and insured. Arizona ROC #365306.

Commercial Electrical Service in the Phoenix Valley

When something electrical fails at a business, the cost is not the repair. It is the register that will not open, the walk-in that is warming up, the tenant calling property management, and the crew standing around waiting. At The Wire Guy Electric, we handle service and maintenance for commercial properties across the Valley: retail centers, offices, restaurants, medical suites, salons, warehouses, and the property managers who look after all of them.

What We Get Called For

  • Power is out in part of the building. Tracing a dead circuit back through the panel, the feeder, or a failed device.
  • Breakers tripping repeatedly. Usually a load problem, a failing breaker, or equipment that has started drawing more than it should.
  • Panel and breaker work. Replacements, additions, and cleanup of panels that have been added to for twenty years without a plan.
  • New equipment circuits. A tenant brings in a new oven, compressor, autoclave, or server rack and the existing circuit will not carry it.
  • Lighting maintenance. Ballasts, drivers, retrofits, and fixtures across a whole property in one visit rather than one at a time.
  • Exterior and parking lot lighting. Pole lights, wall packs, photocells, and timers, which matter for both safety and liability.
  • Exit and emergency lighting. Testing, battery replacement, and bringing a building back into shape before an inspection.
  • Outlets, switches, and devices. The unglamorous list that keeps a space usable.

Service Calls and Response

We keep commercial service work scheduled so businesses are not waiting a week for somebody to look at a dead circuit. For anything that stops operations, we prioritize accordingly.

We also work after hours when the work requires it. Killing power to a shared panel during business hours is rarely the right answer in an occupied center, and for retail and restaurants it is usually not an option at all. If the job needs a Sunday morning or a 6 a.m. start, that is a scheduling question rather than a problem.

For Property Managers and Multi-Site Operators

If you manage several properties, the thing that saves you time is not the hourly rate. It is having one electrician who already knows where the panels are, which suites share distribution, and what was done last time.

We are set up for that: consistent crews, documentation of what we did and where, and a single point of contact rather than a dispatch queue. For recurring needs like lighting sweeps, exit and emergency testing, and seasonal exterior lighting checks, we would rather schedule the work ahead than react to it.

Preventive Work That Is Actually Worth Doing

Most commercial electrical failures announce themselves. The ones we find on a walkthrough, before they take anything down:

  • Hot spots and loose connections at panels and disconnects, which are the leading cause of the failures nobody sees coming
  • Panels that are full, mislabeled, or holding breakers that do not belong in them
  • Corrosion on exterior equipment, especially after monsoon season
  • Exit and emergency fixtures with dead batteries, which is the item most likely to fail an inspection
  • Extension cords and power strips doing the job a dedicated circuit should be doing
